articles.title_orig: Why Russia and China aren't really best friends
articles.title_zh: Why Russia and China aren't really best friends
articles.content_orig:
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Russia's growing dependence on China is reshaping one of the world's most important geopolitical relationships. Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the resulting Western sanctions, Russia has relied heavily on Beijing for trade, technology and critical imports. Along the vast Russia-China border, economic cooperation is expanding, but experts warn that the relationship is increasingly unequal, giving China significant leverage.
DW explores historical tensions, Russian security concerns, reports of espionage and the strategic risks facing Russia as China's influence grows, raising questions about the future of the countries' much-publicized "no-limits" partnership.

articles.title_orig: Dow falls 400 points weighed by Home Depot; Nasdaq slides ahead of Nvidia earnings: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow falls 400 points weighed by Home Depot; Nasdaq slides ahead of Nvidia earnings: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex. Traders, for the moment, must content themselves with the comparatively mundane business of Tuesday's earnings, and options traders are expecting big moves.
With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters.
Implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Nvidia vol reached a multi-year high above 92 in the aftermath of President Trump's tariff Liberation day in April '25. In other words, the company that for much of the AI boom was the most reliable winner in the market, is now more volatile than all but 35 companies in the S&P 500.
"Longer term, I see significant downside risk unless Nvidia can attract an exceptional leader, someone like Tim Cook or AMD's Lisa Su," Nigam Arora, founder of the Arora report, said in a text ahead of the company's after-market report on Tuesday.
Since hitting all-time highs in October, Nvidia shares have fallen 35%, shedding $2 trillion in market capitalization along the way. Including Nvidia, there are only five companies in the S&P 500 worth more than $2 trillion. However, there is evidence that bulls have been holding out hope while bears snatch up profits: the ratio of open puts to call contracts has actually widened towards calls, according to Barchart data. The ratio is currently 0.87, down from a one-year high of 1.02 two weeks ago and the lowest since the first week of October.
The most popular contract by volume on Monday was the 155-strike put expiring at the bell Monday, but the most popular trade for later expiry was the 160-strike call expiring Thursday, and the second-most-common purchase was the 190-strike call expiring Friday, SpotGamma data show.
One catch is that most call contracts traded Monday looked like neutral to bearish positions opened by traders selling calls. Of the 5 million options traded on Monday, 3 million were calls, but more were likely opened by sellers than buyers. Of the $2.3 billion in options premium traded on Nvidia Monday, $1.2 billion was tied to puts, SpotGamma data show.
With bears taking profits in puts the past month, there's another potential snag on open interest. There are very few open put contracts at or below the $157 level at which the stock closed Monday. That suggests any bad surprise would find many traders with little downside protection.
By the same token, there's notable open interest in call contracts from the 175-strike and above, suggesting profit-taking on a bounce could limit Nvidia's recovery past levels it breached over the past week.
Either way, Tuesday's earnings could provide fireworks.

articles.title_orig: Trump arrives in Manila for Quad talks ahead of China visit
articles.title_zh: Trump arrives in Manila for Quad talks ahead of China visit
articles.content_orig:
Tuesday, November 17, 2026 75° Today's Paper
By Mikhail Flores, Karen Lema, Nestor Corrales and Trevor Hunnicutt / Reuters
President Donald Trump waves U.S. and Philippine flags, which he received from a child, after disembarking Air Force One upon arrival at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport to attend the ASEAN-U.S. Summit in Pasay City, Metro Manila, Philippines, today.
MANILA >> President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines today at the tail end of a Southeast Asian summit, with protests awaiting him as he prepares for the first meeting in two years of the Quad group of Indo-Pacific countries.
Trump’s Asia trip, which includes the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen and a much-anticipated trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, comes after his Republican Party’s defeat in midterm elections, plus spy allegations and new U.S. curbs on China’s access to AI chips that could complicate a fragile trade-war truce.
Demonstrators gathered in Manila for a fifth day of protests that have included the burning of Trump effigies, calls for an end to the Middle East war and the scrapping of the U.S.-led Pax Silica supply chain initiative.
Wearing a dark suit, Trump walked down the steps of Air Force One, sometimes raising his hand with a clenched fist as he greeted the waiting honour guard and dancers in traditional Philippine attire. The president’s signature campaign rally song, the Village People’s “YMCA,” played in the background and Trump twirled briefly to the music before heading to his helicopter, Marine One.
Trump arrived at the end of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit and will join a U.S.-ASEAN “Special Summit” later today.
He will first hold a meeting of the Quad – the U.S., Japan, Australia and India – which last convened two years ago. It will be Trump’s first time with the grouping, which his predecessor Joe Biden regarded as a signature foreign policy initiative.
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
It comes ahead of the APEC gathering hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping, who has previously objected to the Quad as an effort to encircle Beijing. Quad members have said the grouping is not directed against any one country.
At the ASEAN summit on Monday, Chinese Premier Li Qiang hailed what he called the “truly extraordinary” economic achievements of China and ASEAN in the face of global trade restrictions, expressing Beijing’s commitment to free trade and the need to “stand united, ward off interference, and work together”.
China is ASEAN’s largest trading partner and a key source of investment, but the biggest economies of the 11-member bloc — which has a combined GDP of more than $3.9 trillion — want to deepen ties with the U.S. despite protracted trade and diplomatic uncertainty under the Trump administration.
Former U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Kurt Campbell credited Washington’s top diplomat, Marco Rubio, with the timing and reconvening of the Quad, which he said had lost ambition under Trump.
“Part of what he (Rubio) is thinking is that this is probably the best possible signal if you’re going to go into a trilateral meeting,” said Campbell, co-founder of The Asia Group, referring to Thursday’s U.S.-China-Russia talks.
“The linchpin of everything that we do in Asia is the U.S.-Japan relationship, and a perception that this is not at the top of the president’s mind would concern me.”
White House spokesperson Olivia Wales on Friday said that under Trump’s leadership, the Quad had demonstrated it is “a partnership of action, tackling the region’s toughest challenges and driving opportunities to ensure a free and open Indo-Pacific”.
A Japanese foreign ministry official said it was expected that Quad leaders would try to show unity, with maritime security, export restrictions, critical-minerals supply-chain diversification and AI among potential discussion points.
Undersea cables, emerging technology and disaster relief were also likely to be covered, a source familiar with the matter said.
ASEAN’s leaders held meetings today involving counterparts from Japan, South Korea, China and India.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi pledged to work with ASEAN to boost regional economic and energy resilience, to address export restrictions and vulnerabilities from rapid AI development, and to strengthen supply chains, including on critical minerals.
“While the international order is experiencing a period of great instability, Japan will play an ever more proactive role,” Takaichi said.
Trump was due to sign a joint statement with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul today on an agreement on reciprocal trade. Thai media have reported the two would hold talks and the statement would be about progress on negotiations.
The U.S. is Thailand’s largest export market, accounting for 24% of its total shipments this year. The U.S. designated Thailand as a major non-NATO ally in 2003.
Trump will meet Ferdinand Marcos Jr, president of U.S. defense ally the Philippines, on Wednesday, before heading to Shenzhen.
Additional reporting by Saurabh Sharma, David Brunnstrom in Washington and Tim Kelly in Tokyo.

articles.title_orig: Trump-Xi meeting looms as US tightens AI chip restrictions on China
articles.title_zh: Trump-Xi meeting looms as US tightens AI chip restrictions on China
articles.content_orig:
Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in May
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of  data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.
But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.
This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress , external , a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".
This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.
One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO .
Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.
The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.
The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.
Batam in Indonesia is emerging as a major regional data centre hub
Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.
But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".
Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.
These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.
But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.
The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.
Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms.
A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure".
Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".
The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.
Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.
Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.
"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.
Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.
The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.
But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.
That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

articles.title_orig: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
articles.title_zh: Tracking China’s War of Words Against Japan
articles.content_orig:
A headline in the Global Times, a newspaper controlled by China’s ruling Communist Party, about Japan’s “remilitarization” after China restricted exports to Japanese entities. Credit... Andy Wong/Associated Press
By Javier C. Hernández and Gal Koplewitz
Javier C. Hernández reported from Tokyo, and Gal Koplewitz from London.
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, met with President Trump at the White House earlier this fall, the two leaders toasted to friendly relations.
But in private, Mr. Xi offered Mr. Trump a stark warning about Japan, a U.S. ally, according to two officials briefed on the talks, who requested anonymity to discuss private conversations. Mr. Xi told Mr. Trump that Japan’s recent military buildup threatened to destabilize Asia, the officials said, and that Mr. Trump should be cautious about working with Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, describing her as a “militarist.”
The warning from Mr. Xi was part of a broader effort by China to isolate and undermine Japan after Ms. Takaichi said last year that Japan could be forced to defend Taiwan in case of a Chinese invasion. China considers Taiwan, a self-governed democracy that lies just 69 miles from Japan’s westernmost island, part of its territory.
Since the comments, Mr. Xi has overseen a campaign involving propaganda and diplomacy to target Japan, according to interviews with officials and scholars, and an analysis by The New York Times of Chinese Foreign Ministry briefings and state media. It is all part of a push, analysts say, to persuade the world that Japan is a resurgent aggressor.
China has deployed words and images to portray Japan as a World War II-era enemy, using phrases like “remilitarization” and “neo-militarism,” and videos that compare Japan to a “rampaging gray rhino.”
Chinese officials have repeatedly sought to belittle Ms. Takaichi, Japan’s first female prime minister, omitting her title in official briefings, breaking with longstanding practice. State media has depicted Ms. Takaichi in short skirts and a nurse’s uniform in cartoons, and described her as “Abe’s girl,” referring to Shinzo Abe, the former Japanese prime minister and Ms. Takaichi’s mentor.
In private conversations with Western scholars, Chinese academics have recently pushed the narrative that Japan is the “Israel of East Asia,” poised to lead the United States into conflict and destabilize the region.
Russia has helped amplify China’s talking points, branding Japan as a threat. Moscow has echoed Beijing in describing Japan as an “ enemy state ” that is not to be trusted, invoking a World War II-era designation used against former Axis powers.
Mr. Xi and Ms. Takaichi will cross paths this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit meeting in Shenzhen, China. The encounter is expected to be frosty; Mr. Xi might try to use the summit as an opportunity to alienate Ms. Takaichi from Japan’s allies, experts say.

articles.title_orig: Bessent vs Lutnick: Who is winning the China chip debate?
articles.title_zh: Bessent vs Lutnick: Who is winning the China chip debate?
articles.content_orig:
A rift between United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over sales of advanced computer chips to China has spilled into public view.
On Monday, the administration of President Donald Trump introduced new rules requiring licences to sell advanced chips to buyers in named third countries suspected of being conduits to China. The new restrictions were written by Bessent’s Department of the Treasury and the White House – not Lutnick’s Department of Commerce, which usually oversees chip exports.
Trump, who is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China’s Shenzhen, has so far not taken a side.
As the US reels from the resignation of chip maker Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang last week over revelations that he had an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, here’s what this all means.
The two cabinet members, who are both veteran investors, disagree over how strictly the US should limit China’s access to the advanced chips that power artificial intelligence (AI).
The US restricts exports of certain advanced AI chips to China. In December 2025, Trump announced that Nvidia could sell its H200 chip to approved Chinese customers, on condition that 25 percent of the revenue would go to the US government. In January, the administration relaxed licensing rules for the H200 and similar chips.
On Monday, new controls were issued to monitor access to US chips in Southeast Asia and Brazil – penned by Bessent with the backing of the National Security Council, not by Lutnick.
As commerce secretary, Lutnick oversees these export controls and is charged with determining which critical technologies US companies can sell abroad, with an eye towards national security.
He has been one of the administration’s most vocal supporters of allowing Nvidia, the world’s dominant maker of AI super chips, to sell to China, despite the fact that it is racing against the US to dominate development of the AI industry.
“You want to sell the Chinese enough that their developers get addicted to the American technology stack,” Lutnick said in July 2025.
But US rules still bar the most advanced chips from being sold to China, and reports of restricted Nvidia chips allegedly being smuggled into the country through unofficial routes have put Lutnick’s role under the microscope.
Lutnick’s department was accused of turning a blind eye to such smuggling and stalling a planned crackdown on actors thought to be involved.
Fellow cabinet members and lawmakers have questioned his department’s handling of the issue, and some lawmakers say it has undermined US national security.
Bessent has pressed for tougher enforcement of existing export rules.
“We have all the authorities that we need. They just need to be implemented,” he said on Friday.
The two men have been rivals for some time. In 2024, Elon Musk and other Trump allies lobbied for Lutnick to get the Treasury job, but it ultimately went to Bessent.
Nvidia controls nearly 90 percent of the market for the most advanced chips used for AI. Worth trillions of dollars, it is among the world’s most valuable companies, and its customers include tech giants Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta.
Nvidia’s cofounder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to an affair with Alice Huang, whom some US officials have suspected of working for Chinese intelligence – a claim denied by China.
Alice Huang is a former senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that builds data centres in Southeast Asia which cater for Chinese clients.
Megaspeed bought more than $4.8bn of Nvidia chips in about two years, but US authorities suspect that many of these chips were then smuggled into China rather than used in Megaspeed’s data centres, a charge it denies.
On Friday, Bessent said four government agencies, including the Treasury, had pushed for months to put Megaspeed on a US trade blacklist, but Lutnick’s Commerce Department had not acted.
“Commerce has the pen,” Bessent told CNBC. “You will have to ask them about their internal processes.”
He also questioned whether Nvidia had properly vetted its customers.
“The real story here should be, did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said.
The new rules require companies to obtain a US licence before shipping advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries Washington suspects of acting as conduit routes for chips to reach China.
It also requires any data centre in the world using Nvidia chips to obtain Washington’s permission before it can “rent” computer power to Chinese customers. This closes a loophole that previously allowed Chinese companies to “rent” the use of advanced chips without purchasing them outright.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the restrictions as “economic coercion” and said Beijing would take “necessary measures” in response.
In Washington, the new restrictions were welcomed by John Moolenaar, the Republican chair of the House Select Committee on China.
The committee, a panel of lawmakers focused on competition with China’s ruling Communist Party, is one of the most hawkish voices on Beijing in Congress. Moolenaar criticised the administration’s decision last year to ease curbs on Nvidia’s chip sales to China.
“Our most advanced AI chips are simply not for sale to our foremost enemy,” he said.
Senior officials including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have argued for keeping the most advanced chips out of China, while lawmakers from both parties have criticised Lutnick.
“It would be dumb and stupid for us to sell that to anybody, especially a country that’s going to reverse-engineer it and leapfrog us,” Rubio said in May.
Greer made a similar case last week, saying that US “crown jewels” should remain in US hands or in the hands of allies.
David Sacks, Trump’s former AI adviser, however, defended selling chips to China and dismissed those pushing for tighter controls.
“The policy of the China hawks is effectively the policy of the CCP [Chinese Communist Party]. Neither one wants American chips in China,” he said in a podcast appearance on Saturday.
On the other side of the political aisle, some Democrats have called for Lutnick to step down from his position for his failure to police chip smuggling.
“Making powerful Nvidia chips available to China through an apparent spy undercut both national security and economic competitiveness,” Senator Richard Blumenthal said in a post on X.
Both Lutnick and Jensen Huang have been summoned to testify before the Senate on December 3.
Trump has swung between restricting and allowing Nvidia’s sales to China. In April 2025, the White House curbed sales of the H20, a chip Nvidia made for the Chinese market – only to agree to allow them three months later.
His later decision in December to permit sales of the more powerful H200 marked a further easing of those restrictions.
Trump has stood by Lutnick, saying on Monday that he was not planning to remove him, days after the Reuters news agency reported that top White House aides had debated whether he should go.
Trump has acknowledged that the issue is splitting his cabinet, without explicitly taking sides.
“It’s a different viewpoint. One wants to be friendly with China and one wants to have a blowup with China,” Trump said. “They both are acceptable, but they are different views.”
Trump has also said it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” for Huang to return to Nvidia .

articles.content_orig:
Laura has led award-winning coverage on the NHS, medical science breakthroughs, and public health policy across the UK for The Telegraph. Her reporting can be found on X: @lauradonnlee
A Viagra-like drug could slow Alzheimer’s disease, its manufacturer’s trial results suggest.
The once-daily pill slowed decline by 31 per cent over a year among patients who were not already taking standard Alzheimer’s medicines.
The benefit was in 604 of 1,535 patients. Across the whole trial, researchers could not establish a significant benefit.
The findings of the international trial, whose lead investigator was based at Stanford University, were presented at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston.
The experimental treatment, called AR1001, contains mirodenafil, a drug developed to treat erectile dysfunction.
It belongs to the same family of medicines as Viagra, but is a different drug, and the findings do not establish that Viagra itself can treat Alzheimer’s.
Researchers believe AR1001 could protect brain cells by acting on several processes involved in Alzheimer’s, including inflammation and changes to the tau protein.
Dr Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer’s Research UK, said: “These are very encouraging results, marking an important milestone in the search for new Alzheimer’s treatments.”
She said the drug was particularly interesting because it was a tablet that worked differently from existing treatments, targeting several processes involved in brain function.
The trial involved 1,535 people with early Alzheimer’s across 13 countries, including Britain.
Participants received either AR1001 or a dummy pill, with researchers tracking their memory, thinking and ability to manage everyday tasks over a year.
The benefit was seen among 604 patients who were not already taking standard Alzheimer’s medicines. In this group, those taking AR1001 deteriorated 31 per cent more slowly than those given the dummy pill.
However, when researchers looked at all 1,535 patients together, including those already taking other Alzheimer’s medicines, they could not establish a significant benefit.
Dr Scales said: “The trial demonstrated a statistically significant slowing of clinical decline in participants who were not taking other commonly used Alzheimer’s medications alongside the trial drug. However, this benefit was not significant across the overall trial group.”
It is not yet clear why the drug worked for patients who were not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines.
These included memantine and medicines known as acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, which are used to treat Alzheimer’s symptoms.
Dr Richard Oakley, associate director for research and innovation at Alzheimer’s Society, said: “These topline results are an exciting sign that we could have a totally new treatment for early Alzheimer’s disease that tackles its causes, not just its symptoms. “It’s fantastic to see research and clinical trials unlocking promising new ways to target Alzheimer’s Disease. AR1001 takes a novel approach, relaxing blood vessels to increase blood flow to the brain. And unlike other disease-modifying treatments that have shown benefit in late-stage trials, it is taken as a once-a-day tablet, which could make treatment simpler.”
Researchers measured deterioration using an 18-point scale assessing memory, judgment and everyday abilities.
Over the year, patients taking AR1001 in the smaller group deteriorated by 0.44 points less than those given the dummy pill.
This represented a 31 per cent reduction in the rate of decline, rather than an improvement in patients’ existing symptoms.
Other tests of thinking and daily functioning also favoured the drug, although several differences were not statistically significant.
Tests of spinal fluid provided evidence that the drug was acting on its intended biological target within the brain and nervous system.
AR1001 blocks an enzyme called PDE5, increasing a chemical signal involved in several processes that researchers believe could help protect brain cells.
Dr Sharon Sha, chief of the Memory Disorders Division at Stanford University and global principal investigator of the trial, said the results among patients not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines were encouraging, as was the drug’s safety record.
She said further research was needed to understand its effects.
“The work of POLARIS-AD is another step towards filling an unmet need in Alzheimer’s disease in which patients need more options for treatment,” she said.
AriBio, the company developing AR1001, plans to discuss the findings with US regulators, a potential step towards seeking approval for the pill as an Alzheimer’s treatment.
Dr David Greeley of AriBio, who led the drug’s earlier Phase 2 trial, said the findings were “very encouraging”.
He said: “If approved, this oral drug would broaden patients’ options.”
He added: “Further evaluation is needed, but our goal is meaningful treatment that not only helps patients but that can be realistically afforded, received and sustained.”
The company said the drug was generally well tolerated, with serious adverse events reported in similar proportions of the treatment and placebo groups.
Diarrhoea, falls and dizziness were among the most common adverse events. About 5 per cent stopped the drug because of adverse events, compared with 2 per cent receiving a placebo.
Most participants who completed the first year entered an extension study, in which everyone received the drug. It is expected to finish next year.
Dr Scales said: “We look forward to seeing whether these benefits are sustained over the longer term.”
Researchers said they closely monitored “unwanted sexual behaviour” during the trial and no significant signal had been reported.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic likely to price IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, sources tell CNBC
articles.title_zh: Anthropic likely to price IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, sources tell CNBC
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic is likely to price its IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, multiple sources told CNBC's David Faber on Tuesday.
The artificial intelligence company is planning to close the order books and lock in total demand at 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Anthropic is slated to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" and start trading on Nov. 19.
If Anthropic's IPO proceeds as planned, the company will debut roughly five months after SpaceX went public in a record offering that raised $85.7 billion. But Anthropic is facing a public market that's grown increasingly skeptical of the AI trade, as well as mounting and widespread antipathy toward the technology in the U.S.
A group of researchers, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , co-founded the company in 2021 after defecting from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it underwent a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code .
For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus . It reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.
Anthropic has long worked to establish a reputation as a safety-conscious AI company, and its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its listing.
"I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video . "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time."
"I invite you to join us on the next phase of this journey," Amodei said.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia’s first big move after Jensen Huang’s exit targets national security
articles.title_zh: Nvidia’s first big move after Jensen Huang’s exit targets national security
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia has formed a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance following the abrupt resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who had links to one of the company’s customers.
Nvidia said Tuesday that the new standing committee will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. The move comes amid increased scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Huang’s alleged ties to the suspected spy and his advocacy for easing restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China.
The Commerce Department said Monday it was planning to introduce new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside of the U.S. in an effort to prevent companies in China and elsewhere from circumventing existing rules by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. The interim rule was made in direct response to the unfolding chip smuggling scandal at Nvidia.
The announcement comes just a few hours before Nvidia’s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings call. Analysts, the media, and shareholders expect the company to address the controversy and outline how it might affect operations. This is the first major action by the company under the leadership of Collette Kress, the company’s CFO who took over as interim CEO after Huang stepped down last week.
The committee, which will meet at least quarterly, will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include fellow directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members.
Nvidia already has a national security team and global trade compliance team. Those teams will now report to this board committee and Kress on day-to-day operations.
Huang has agreed to testify before Congress later this month.

articles.title_orig: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
articles.title_zh: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
articles.content_orig:
Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all.
The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user’s knowledge.
Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent’s reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”
The NewCore employees sent the gateway logs to Grok Bot support personnel and asked what was causing the bots to access accounts without prompting or approval. The support team’s reply indicated the behavior was by design and intended to allow the bots to proactively take actions on behalf of users. In other words, the unrequested and unlogged access attempts were a feature designed to make Grok Bot more useful by periodically checking in and finding tasks to perform before a user even asks. The proactive check-in is a feature of Cursor, the AI coding service SpaceXSI recently acquired.
“There is no bug to patch, which is exactly why this is worse than a bug,” Ido Hoorvitch, a NewCore security researcher, wrote in an email. “A vulnerability gets fixed. This is the product working as designed: an agent that holds your credentials, acts under your identity while you sleep, ignores the one refusal you can give it, and then tells you it did nothing.”
Hoorvitch said that Grok Bot provides minimal notification of the automatic “turns,” or the cycles that occur when an agent receives instructions or context, decides what to do, and calls whatever tools it chooses. The notice comes during onboarding when the bot says it keeps working while the user is away from the computer and connects to apps and uses them the way the user does.
“It reads like a welcome message and scrolls off the screen in under a minute,” Hoorvitch said. “Nobody is asked to consent to it. Nothing says the platform will start turns with no message from you, or that those turns will use your connectors.”
The researcher said that Grok Bot documentation notes that a primary bot checks in on its own, and a changelog mentions brief background wakes, but there is no mention that the check-ins “reach into your connected apps.” Further, once a check-in runs, there is no mention of it in the chat interface or in the chat history, and as already noted, prompts to stop check-ins don’t work. Hoorvitch said the bot “always asks before making changes,” but that applies only to events in which data or changes are written to an app.
NewCore contacted Grok Bot support on November 4. At the time, users had no way to turn off the automatic check-ins. Then, eight days later, Hoorvitch said, the Cursor dashboard, the administrative console behind Grok Bot, received an update. Under bot capabilities, a new toggle called proactive messages appeared. By default, it’s set to on. When a team admin sets it to off, bots no longer run check-ins on their own.
SpaceXSI representatives didn’t answer questions sent by email.

articles.title_orig: Treasury finalizes 401(k) auto-enrollment rules that could boost retirement savings
articles.title_zh: Treasury finalizes 401(k) auto-enrollment rules that could boost retirement savings
articles.content_orig:
The 2027 contribution limit for 401(k) plans is rising to $25,500, up $1,000 from 2026’s $24,500 cap.
The Treasury Department and IRS have issued final regulations requiring automatic enrollment in certain workplace retirement plans, implementing a provision of the SECURE 2.0 Act aimed at expanding retirement savings.
Treasury estimates the law's automatic-enrollment expansion will increase retirement savings by an average of $4.2 billion annually over the 2023–2032 period.
The rules cover certain 401(k) and 403(b) retirement plans, outlining how eligible employees will automatically contribute a portion of their pay unless they choose otherwise.
Under the final regulations, covered plans generally must automatically enroll eligible employees at a contribution rate of 3% of pay. After an initial participation period, the default rate generally must rise by at least one percentage point annually until it reaches at least 10%, subject to a 15% maximum.
JPMORGAN CHASE SYSTEMS RECOVERING FOLLOWING HOURSLONG NATIONWIDE TECHNICAL OUTAGE
The U.S. Treasury building in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Aug. 5, 2025. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Employees can opt out or choose a different contribution rate.
The final regulations generally apply to retirement plan years beginning after Dec. 31, 2027, giving employers time to make administrative changes, Treasury said.
"A financially secure retirement is a cornerstone of the American Dream, and every worker deserves the opportunity to achieve it," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the release.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaking from the Cash Room at the Treasury Department on August 24, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images / Getty Images)
"Today’s rules help more American families and workers build retirement savings while keeping them in control of their contributions, and give employers the clarity and flexibility to invest in their employees’ futures."
The department said the regulations clarify statutory exceptions for qualifying small and new businesses, governmental plans, church plans and SIMPLE 401(k) plans.
Employers also receive flexibility in the timing and amount of automatic contribution increases, within the law’s limits.
The Treasury Building in Washington, D.C. (Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto via Getty Images / Getty Images)
The regulations allow certain required notices to be combined and reduce annual notice requirements for qualifying employees who are not participating. Those employees must still receive annual reminders and any plan documents they are entitled to request.

articles.title_orig: American shoppers are showing signs of strain heading into the holiday season
articles.title_zh: American shoppers are showing signs of strain heading into the holiday season
articles.content_orig:
Americans pulled back on some purchases last month, as  high gas prices and ongoing cost-of-living concerns continued to weigh on some household budgets, new data showed Tuesday.
US retail sales rose 0.2% in October, a slowdown after gas prices drove a 0.8% gain the month before, according to Commerce Department data released Tuesday.
October’s spending tally was driven lower by a drop in car sales, which offset a more modest uptick in gasoline station sales (which slowed to a gain of 1.5% versus a 6% increase the month before), data showed.
Retail sales are adjusted for seasonal swings but not inflation, which rose 0.4% in October, Consumer Price Index data shows.
In addition to falling sales of cars, Tuesday report showed consumers reined in purchases on furniture, sporting goods and apparel; and cut back a little on their food spending.
October’s tepid spending, however, could be a sign that some consumers may be gearing up for the holiday shopping season, said Elizabeth Renter, lead economist at Life360.
“Several of the categories where spending declined are discretionary categories – purchases you can put off for a while because you don’t need those goods every single month,” she wrote in a note Tuesday. “Because this is October data, savvy families may be saving those purchases for holiday sale deals.”
To be sure, a closely watched category of spending that strips out some more volatile areas (such as gasoline stations, auto sales, building materials and restaurants) rose at a stronger-than-expected rate of 0.6%, a tick higher than a 0.5% gain notched in September.
Sales at miscellaneous stores (a catch-all category that includes retailers in pet supplies, office goods, florists etc.) saw the biggest gains in October, at 4.7%, while spending remained firm at health and personal care stores as well as online retailers (Amazon, for example, held a sales event early last month).
“We wouldn’t say consumers are splurging, but they certainly aren’t retrenching,” Oren Klachkin, Nationwide financial markets economist, wrote in a note to investors Tuesday. “High prices and interest rates are making some trade down and be more judicious, but solid fundamentals and a boost from early holiday shopping are keeping consumers in a spending mood.”
Tuesday’s report underscored the ongoing bifurcation of household finances, ING chief international economist James Knightley said, noting the differing trajectories of spending among high-income individuals versus middle- and lower-income Americans.
“Middle- and lower-income households tend to spend more of their income of physical goods, such as food and clothing, and squeezed spending power limits the potential for growth,” he wrote. “Conversely, high income households have seen their wealth surge, boosting consumption, and are accounting for a growing share of total consumer spending.”
In addition to Tuesday’s retail sales data, a fuller picture of consumer health and spending could come via Target and Walmart, which are slated to release their latest earnings reports on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively, this week.
This story is developing and will be updated.

articles.title_orig: Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed gov won't attend Trump committee's hearing
articles.title_zh: Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed gov won't attend Trump committee's hearing
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook 's attorney on Tuesday gave the strongest signal yet that his client will not attend a hearing at the White House with a "committee of inquiry" investigating mortgage fraud allegations against Cook.
The committee established last month by President Donald Trump , who has previously tried to remove Cook from the central bank's board, is pretextual and poses a threat to the Fed, attorney Abbe Lowell wrote in a letter to presidential counsel Will Scharf.
"Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence," Lowell wrote in the letter, which is dated Monday and was made public Tuesday.
The latest correspondence came nearly two weeks after the White House committee delayed its proposed hearing with Cook to Dec. 14 from Nov. 5. Lowell said that any hearing with Cook could not take place until at least December because of conflicts with her Fed duties.
While Lowell had raised strong concerns from the outset about the legitimacy of the committee, he initially said Cook "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name."
But he has continued to cast doubts on both the committee's purpose and its composition of three executive branch officials, including National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett .
Lowell's tone sounded more hostile than ever in this week's letter, the first known to be sent by either party in the matter since the Republican Party's devastating losses in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
He accused Scharf and the committee of seeking "only to manufacture 'cause' for a predetermined removal outcome."
Lowell highlighted two top concerns. First, he asserted that Hassett "is not competent to serve on any factfinding committee" because his prior comments about Cook "demonstrate that he has prejudged the issue."
Second, Lowell called it "fundamentally unfair" that the committee is demanding Cook hand over documents "immediately," while pledging to provide the governor with its own records just seven days before the hearing.
"Your and the Committee's failure to address these legitimate issues, over multiple weeks of back-and-forth correspondence, reinforces my prior observation: President Trump's decision to fire Governor Cook has already been made," Lowell wrote.
"Consequently, this Committee process appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook or to unreasonably manufacture a supposed 'adverse inference' if she does not participate in a process that does not comport with the requirements of a fair hearing," the lawyer wrote.
Lowell told Scharf that Cook would still be prepared to appear for a hearing if the White House "implements fair procedures." But the "ultimatums" Scharf gave in his last reply in early November "do not provide a productive path forward to enabling that participation," Lowell wrote.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Lowell's letter.
Trump, who frequently urges the Fed to lower interest rates, has long sought to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden .
Cook, the first Black woman to serve on the Fed's Board of Governors, last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its meeting in September.
Trump officials sent a criminal referral last year alleging Cook may have committed mortgage fraud by falsely claiming different properties as her primary residence in order to get more favorable terms. Cook adamantly denied wrongdoing, and, after Trump tried to fire her in August 2025, filed a lawsuit to block her removal.
The Supreme Court in June prevented Trump from firing Cook, but gave him a path to try again if additional legal steps were taken. In August, the White House told Cook it was reviving its efforts to fire her on mortgage-related grounds. In October, Trump signed a presidential memo establishing the committee of inquiry to investigate allegations that Cook lied on records related to "one or more mortgage instruments."

articles.title_orig: FAA, Microsoft, banks: Why it feels like everything keeps breaking
articles.title_zh: FAA, Microsoft, banks: Why it feels like everything keeps breaking
articles.content_orig:
Maybe the trouble started with the AI billionaire and the Silicon Valley uproar that followed talk of his infidelity, including with an alleged Chinese spy. Or maybe it was the Microsoft outage that, depending on how you looked at it, either cast millions of frustrated workers adrift or spared them from a daily, unrelenting electronic avalanche.
Then, just as it seemed things were calming down after a weekend of airline chaos, United Airlines announced a widespread outage Monday afternoon and several top U.S. banks began reporting significant slowdowns, with transactions sometimes not going through.
"We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible," a Chase spokesperson said in a statement.
America has been hearing that for days. From seemingly everywhere.
The prime example began Friday afternoon, when U.S. aviation authorities ordered the grounding of planes across the country. That was when many began to think that something was up.
Just ask Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, New Jersey, trying to fly out of Newark Liberty International Airport when his canceled flight led to a few beers with his brother in an airport bar and eventually a night in a hotel. Saturday morning, he was back at the airport to try again.
"There's a lot of weird stuff going on," Amasio said. "It makes one think."
His first thought was dark: "We talk about how wars aren't done with bombs anymore. They shut down airspace or a power grid. They can cripple an economy."
Throw in a few more examples just from Friday — a cruise ship that overturned in New Orleans when a tanker slammed into it, suspicious drones over a U.S. air base in Britain, a bomb found near an ethanol plant in Illinois — and perhaps things seem even weirder, opening the door for a writer who has been picking at America's fears for generations to offer his own explanation.
"The aliens have landed," Stephen King wrote in a Friday afternoon post on the social platform X. "That's the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don't want to start a worldwide panic."
The official explanations for the thousands of grounded jetliners and hours of email and other computer troubles were far more prosaic.
A technology upgrade on the nation's air traffic control system had overloaded antiquated equipment and caused "intermittent" communications and radar gaps, leading to the ground stop that lasted more than four hours, administration officials said.
By Saturday morning, air travel was already smoother and Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said airline schedules should be back to normal by late Sunday.
Microsoft, for its part, said Saturday that its services had been fully restored, saying the problem "was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced" following a recent network change.
The outage is believed to have affected many millions of people around the world. The banking problems began after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects through the financial system.
On Monday, United said its tech problem was affecting departing flights, not planes in the air.
Chase said its problems were not the result of a cyberattack, and it was working to bring services back online.
Maxine Gustafson, a 34-year-old physician assistant from Minneapolis, was in line to pick up a hastily booked rental car at Chicago's O'Hare airport on Friday afternoon so she and colleagues could get home from a work training.
Gustafson said the week's mishaps made her feel afraid and helpless.
"It makes you think, like, is this a cyberattack?" she said. "We don't have control over a lot of this stuff."
Both the FAA and Microsoft said there were no signs that malicious activity had been behind the troubles.
Tori Perkins, 34, was hoping for a Saturday flight at Terminal 2 at San Diego International Airport, where 11 of the 62 flights already were listed as canceled that morning and the same number were delayed. Crowds were normal.
"It's one of those things where I don't necessarily believe what the government says," said Perkins, who seemed to take the setback in stride. "I don't know what's true because there are so many people saying different things."
Perkins, who lives in Hawaii, was in San Diego on a layover on her way to see family in Florida. She spent Friday night at the airport.
She was not surprised that Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy had made a plea Friday for tens of billions in more funding to upgrade the country's notoriously outdated air traffic system.
"It sounds like more of the same," she said.
The FAA has already replaced thousands of copper wire connections with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. The White House has been pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Sometimes chaos brings out the best in people.
Corbyn Wascher was stuck on the tarmac at Charlotte Douglas International Airport for four hours while heading back to Moline, Illinois, from Miami, where he had been at an education conference.
He said everyone was cordial on the plane, talking to one another and stretching their legs. He was impressed with the American Airlines staff, who handed out water, pretzels and biscotti snacks, though they were clearly under stress.
"The stewardesses were amazing," said the 37-year-old high school teacher.
Back at the Newark airport, Caroline Ruiz had caught a few hours of sleep by a heating vent. She wasn't sure what time it was as she waited for someone to bring her a meal she was promised after the cancellation of the first leg of her 24-hour trip to Australia. She hoped to get started later Saturday.
It was two days in a row, she noted, where she had been betrayed by technology.
Though maybe one of those days didn't count as a betrayal.
"I kind of got a free day yesterday" because the Microsoft systems were down. __
This story has been updated to correct that a bomb was found near an ethanol plant in Illinois, not Ohio. ___
Associated Press journalists Elliot Spagat in San Diego, Ali Swenson in Chicago, Jessica Hill in Las Vegas and Aron Ranen in Newark contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Glasses and shirt buttons will be examined to stop cheating in South Korea's college entrance exams
articles.title_zh: Glasses and shirt buttons will be examined to stop cheating in South Korea's college entrance exams
articles.content_orig:
South Korea will inspect all glasses worn by students taking its national college entrance exam this week, after the top scorer on another notoriously difficult test confessed he used AI to cheat, shaking confidence in the country’s strict examination process.
The cheating scandal prompted Prime Minister Han Sung-sook to call officials to a meeting on Monday, where the country’s education ministry was ordered to ensure test takers hand in their smart devices before exams.
Education minister Choi Kyo-jin told parliament there would be “a thorough inspection of all glasses in each test session to ensure a fair and safe testing environment.” Smart glasses have been added to a list of items prohibited inside the testing room, he said, adding that the consequences of cheating using smart devices could include criminal punishment.
This Thursday, around 550,000 students are expected to sit the country’s infamous College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT) , an arduous eight-hour exam that is seen as a barometer for future success and social status in hyper-competitive South Korea.
Inside the ‘world’s toughest’ college entry exam
Each year the test brings the country to a standstill, with flights banned from taking off or landing during the half-hour-long listening comprehension section to ensure there are no distractions.
The changes to exam rules come one day after the top scoring student in the country’s accounting exam confessed to cheating, following months of scrutiny over his suspiciously high score.
In a video published online Sunday, the student said he had cheated using a miniature camera, his phone and AI, adding he had confessed to Seoul police about the fraud.
“I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” he said in the video.
He referenced the upcoming college entrance exam, warning “if there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”
Students have found ways to cheat on tests since the dawn of time, but the rise of AI has made deception slicker and more sophisticated. Smart glasses with integrated AI engines, built-in cameras, microphones, speakers and sensors have become tools for cheating.
While old-fashioned cheating may have required craning your neck for a quick peek at your neighbor’s answers, a test taker wearing AI glasses can simply glance at a question and have the answer fed back to them in a matter of seconds.
Once reserved for tech nerds, the devices are quickly moving into the mainstream. US tech giant Meta launched its first AI-enabled glasses with Ray-Ban in late 2023 , and has since released several new versions. Last year alone, more than seven million pairs were sold.
The new technology has become especially problematic in East Asia’s test-obsessed societies, where students have turned to smart glasses and AI glasses to get an upper hand, forcing governments to take strict measures.
Earlier this year in South Korea, two students taking an exam to assess their English language skills — the results of which are often used to make hiring decisions — were caught using smart glasses.
In Taiwan, a student sitting for an entrance exam for a top medical school was discovered wearing smart glasses after proctors noticed the student staring oddly at the test, leading to an inspection that revealed the frame was emitting heat.
For China’s grueling annual college entrance exam in June – which more than 10 million hopefuls take each year – authorities required screening of all glasses.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia shares set for $335 billion swing after earnings, options show
articles.title_zh: Nvidia shares set for $335 billion swing after earnings, options show
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia reports Tuesday with its longtime finance chief, Colette Kress , in charge. The Bank of Nvidia she inherited was already turning customers away.
Wall Street will grade Nvidia ( NVDA ) on chips and guidance after the bell . But the most revealing page may sit in the back of the filing, where Nvidia lists what it has promised to pay or guarantee for others.
That list nearly doubled in a single quarter, JPMorgan's Michael Cembalest noted , and comes to about $530 billion with guarantees included. Huang's exit put that web of deals under the microscope.
The man who built the bank had already started closing its windows.
In August, Nvidia's guarantee for OpenAI's Ohio data center came in at less than half the $250 billion that had been discussed. By the end of the month, Nvidia had paused revenue-sharing deals with neoclouds — upstart cloud companies that rent out Nvidia chips — The Wall Street Journal reported . In October, Huang told those partners to get their customers to pay upfront.
"You're not charging what you should be charging," he told them at a conference in Berlin, according to the Journal.
Neoclouds may be rooting for a Huang comeback , but his return wouldn't reopen windows he was shutting himself. Kress is expected to tighten the purse strings even further, the Journal reported. The $500 billion lending platform Nvidia launched with Wall Street in August still hasn't closed a deal, and lenders want Nvidia to back more than a quarter of each loan, Bloomberg reported.
"I do expect the company to pivot pretty hard under new leadership," Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, said on Yahoo Finance's Market Hang. "I think we're going to see less circular financing activity. We've already seen a slowdown just in the last three weeks."
The stock market noticed first. CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Nebius ( NBIS ) have each lost more than half their value in three months, while Nvidia is down about 30%. Nebius is still up for the year.
Some promises can't be taken back. Deals Nvidia already signed — from chip supply orders to cloud capacity it agreed to rent back — are still owed. And Nvidia is set to buy $10 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the AI lab's IPO , which prices Wednesday, according to Anthropic's amended filing.
That makes Tuesday's report about more than demand. Investors will want to know whether the pile of promises keeps growing, and whether Kress sounds like a banker who's still lending.
David Nelson, chief strategist at Belpointe Asset Management, sees two AI trades hiding inside one. Some companies pay for their data centers out of the cash they earn. Others lean on leases, loan guarantees and "other people's money," as he put it, the kind of help Nvidia has been handing out.
"They have been priced as one trade," he wrote Monday. "They won't be much longer."

articles.title_zh: Deutsche Bank Leak Reveals $582 Million In Epstein Payments, Accidental Trump Tax Disclosure
articles.content_orig:
Deutsche Bank’s headquarters in Frankfurt. The bank long resisted breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under President Vladimir V. Putin. Credit... Felix Schmitt for The New York Times
By Russ Buettner Khadija Sharife Brian Fitzpatrick Frederik Obermaier Bastian Obermayer and Sophia Baumann
When Russian missiles began pummeling Ukraine in February 2022, executives at one of the world’s largest banks sensed trouble headed their way.
Within hours of an invasion that set off a war that is now in its fifth year, Western governments issued new financial sanctions intended to further isolate Russia from the world economy.
At Deutsche Bank, a longtime bank of Russian industry titans and oligarchs, officials scrambled to get ahead of the damage. “Russian Sanctions Urgent Request” read the subject line of an email sent by one of Deutsche’s anti-financial crime specialists to her colleagues.
“As you know we have a large Russian Oligarchs client population” and other clients with investments in Russian companies, she wrote. She asked which of those clients “we potentially could unwind and which not.” Should the bank advise them, she wondered, to withdraw their money “while they still can?”
This email exchange was the beginning of a frenzied reckoning within the scandal-plagued bank over its long resistance to breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under Vladimir V. Putin, the Russian president. The bank’s clients included the Russian billionaires Oleg V. Deripaska and Viktor F. Vekselberg. Time and again over many years, records show, Deutsche Bank’s risk managers warned that such relationships were perilous.
But profits associated with maintaining its Russian clients won out every time.
Russia’s war in Ukraine swept up Deutsche Bank in a larger shift. For decades, German politicians and business leaders believed that working with Russia and deepening economic ties between the two countries would discourage Russian aggression. That strategy collapsed after the invasion.

articles.title_orig: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Putin's Crimea bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack.
The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Putin in 2018.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
The damage after the overnight attack, involving missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were operating.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - were closed after Russia hit Ukraine's capital overnight.
Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Strikes on the busy Northern and Southern Bridges will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.
Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.title_orig: Mongolia’s president says he will step down after facing accusations of corruption
articles.title_zh: Mongolia’s president says he will step down after facing accusations of corruption
articles.content_orig:
Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa said Tuesday that he would resign after the opposition Democratic Party accused him of profiting from a government railway project.
At a press conference, Khurelsukh said he was being "falsely accused and defamed" but would resign in order to "restore my good name."
He has pledged to cooperate with investigators.
Before the resignation takes effect, it must first be accepted by parliament, the State Great Khural.
Nyambaatar Khishgee, the ex-mayor of Ulaanbaatar, the country's capital, on Saturday accused Khurelsukh of receiving $25 million (around €23 million) linked to the Tavantolgoi-Gashuunsukhait railway project.
The railway connects the Tavantolgoi coal mine with the Mongolian port of Gashuunsukhait on the Chinese border, a central hub for the export of coal from Mongolia to China.
The former mayor belongs to the president's party, but is part of a different faction within it.
The opposition Democratic Party picked up on the accusations and called on Khurelsukh to step down.
According to the allegations, Khurelsukh received the money in bribes from the conglomerate Bodi International LLC, which received the contract to construct the railway without a competitive tender.
Bodi on Monday denied having paid any cash bribes to obtain the contract.
Khurelsukh, from the Mongolian People's Party, has been president since 2021.
But infighting has caused disruption in the party in recent years, with three prime ministers taking office in just nine months.
Khurelsukh paid a state visit to Germany from October 19 to 22 this year.

articles.title_orig: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.title_zh: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.content_orig:
The UK has sanctioned companies it said were involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.
The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.
Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months.
It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the E1 area east of Jerusalem.
The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".
The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.
It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.
The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of settlement goods and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.
Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.
"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.
"The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.
"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."
In September, the UK government announced that it would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as acting against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.
At the time, Miliband said the move marked the "beginning of a new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering but acts".
The announcement prompted a furious reaction from Israel .
Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.
There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
